header.title: Regula Ad Monachos: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Ferreolus Ucetienses Episcopus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp1093.tmp1093.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1093.tmp1093.opp-lat: Line 1: 'scin' read as 'se in'. Ch. V: 'anquantu(??)um' is garbled; read as 'aliquantulum' (somewhat). 'Nec ... adjiciat' in ch. V is obscure; rendered as a further question about his motive. 'Pernoctatum tempus' probably corrupt for 'praenotatum' (appointed). 'Crudelitatis' may be corrupt (perhaps 'credulitatis' or similar). Ch. IV: 'quis hoste publico et secreta pugna vincatur' is obscure and probably corrupt. Ch. VI: 'lanium' read as 'tandem/tunc'; the closing 'Si tamen credi...' is elliptical. Ch. VIII: 'ne jactantia cadat sui, propter Deum sublimitas deponatur' and 'Quid humile inest profectus in capite' are corrupt; translated tentatively. Psalm reference in ch. VII given as cx in the edition; the verse is Ps. 100(101).

Ch. XI: 'bis' read as 'his'. Ch. XII: the sentence is awkward and possibly corrupt; 'quantum' seems to need a verb understood. Ch. XIV: 'Luc. vii' is the edition's reference (the saying is at Luke ix); '(??)ocatus' read as 'vocatus'. Ch. XVII: 'formarius' is a rare office, apparently an instructor or exemplar of discipline beneath the prior; the sense is uncertain. Ch. XIX: 'curo' read as 'cum'; the citation 'II Thes. iii' is the edition's (the verse is II Tim. iii). Ch. XX: the last sentence ('velut contemptorem placuit revocare') is terse; the sense may be that he is to be recalled and treated as a despiser [of the rule].

Ch. XXIII: the first quotation, attributed to 'the blessed apostle' and referenced 'Luc. v', is James 5:12. Ch. XXIV: 'publicanum' (publican, i.e. tax-collector) seems odd in context and may be a corruption, perhaps for a word meaning buffoon; 'servandum mundo' read as 'servandum mando'; 'ne in aliquo discretionis creat disciplina' is corrupt, read as 'careat' ('lack discretion'). Ch. XXVI: 'mons est' read as 'mos est'; the final sentence about the harvest ('orbe solis ardor ebiberit ... messura ejus evaserit') is obscure and the rendering is tentative. Ch. XXVII: 'sil publicos' read as 'sit publicus'; 'aut rogans praesumat' read as 'aut rogans aut rogatus praesumat'. Ch. XXVIII: the quotation is 2 Thess. 3:10, unreferenced in the text.

30.head: 'absque voluntate nihil operis faciat' ('opens' read as 'operis') is elliptical; the chapter shows the sense is that the abbot is not bound to manual work except by his own choice. 31: 'vehit impiger f semper debellator afficiet' read as 'velut impiger semper debellator afficiat'; the sense requires a negative ('so that it does not fight'), supplied in brackets. 32: 'multos astrictus habeat' seems to lack a noun (perhaps 'nodos', knots). 33: 'ut animo et non lecto' read as 'ut uno lecto non'; 'decipiatur ab (??)' is damaged, perhaps 'a somno' (by sleep); 'liniandum' read as 'implendum'. 34: 'vilia' read as 'vitia' (vices); the quotation attributed to Ephesians 4 is in fact 1 Cor. 7:20/24. 35: 'lusus fuerit' probably for 'ausus fuerit' (dared).

The text has many scanning errors, silently corrected: Ui = Ut, priest = praeest, Hie = ne, mendacium se-etantem = mendacium sectantem, monilis = monitis, audsle = audite, reliqueram = reliquerant. Several scriptural quotations in 36.2 are damaged; I supplied the evident Vulgate wording in brackets ('yourself and to teaching', 'yourself', 'I will give'). In the I Peter quotation, 'qua incipiet revelati gloriae' is corrupt; it is translated as 'the glory that is to be revealed'. 'et ire ostende' is probably corrupt for 'et tu ostende'; translated as an imperative. In 38.3 the verbs 'revocemur ... deponam' are evidently errors for third-person plurals and are translated as such. The quotation attributed to Isaiah is in fact from Jeremiah viii, as the reference shows. The references 'II Tim. iv' (actually I Tim. iv.16), 'Rom. iv' (Rom. xiv) and 'II Tim. iii' (I Tim. v.23) are as printed in the edition, except that Rom. xiv has been corrected in the translation. In 38.5, 'quod longe etiam a monachis' is elliptical.

38.7: 'fletum' is read as 'fictum' (feigned); 'impium' as 'impius'. 38.8: 'secundum flagello subdi' is unclear, perhaps a corruption (e.g. 'secundo', 'a second time', or a lost noun after 'secundum'); rendered loosely as 'subjected to the lash'. 'Fartum' read as 'Furtum'. The psalm quoted is Ps. xlix (Vulgate) though the edition gives xliii; the Colossians reference reads 'Col. m' for iii.

nodes.text: The Rule of Saint Ferreolus, Bishop of Uzès, for Monks.

The beginning of the Rule concerning those things which I, as founder, have laid down to be observed by the monks of the monastery of Ferreolus; praying that, with the Lord's help, these sons whom I have begotten for the Lord through faith, keeping these things with their whole mind and holy intent, may by the best and most perfect course of life do violence to heaven, as it is written, and prepare for themselves the mansions prepared for worthy inhabitants. And so may it come about that, following the Lamb wherever he goes, they despise present things for this purpose, that they may seize upon the things to come.
Chapter One. On obedience.

First, that the monk, whose proper task it is to build up many virtues in himself, should lay in himself the foundation of obedience: so that he may fulfil those things which the blessed Apostle admonishes us to observe, when he commands, saying: Obey those set over you, and be subject to them; for they keep watch as men who are to render account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not groaning; for this is profitable to you (Hebr. xiii).
Chapter II. On reverence, how great is to be kept.

That reverence be kept by all toward the abbot in every way with love; so that love may show concord, and fear may know discipline. For rightly is he feared as a lord and loved as a father, to whom, the flock of the holy congregation having been entrusted, the care of souls is properly committed: whom the charge committed to him daily, along that road which is unavoidable for those who are to die, either drags to punishment or leads to glory; as Scripture says: To whom more is entrusted, from him assuredly more is required (Luke xii). Likewise also the Gospel reveals the truth to us through the likeness of a parable, where we read that the Lord handed over five talents to a servant; and because he gained five more besides, he deserves to hear from the Lord: Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful to me over a few things, I will set you over many: enter into the joy of your Lord (Matth. xxv).
Chap. III. On charity.

In the third place, on account of the very sacred number of the Trinity, we have thought it right to insert charity, the mother of all virtues, which the Apostle follows with such praise before all the virtues: Charity does not act wrongly; charity never fails (I Cor. xiii); and again: Charity covers a multitude of sins (I Pet. iv). It is fitting therefore for monks to cleave to this precept, so that, according to the blessed Apostle, many may be made one body in Christ (I Cor. xii), and that may be fulfilled in them which the reading of the Acts of the Apostles, setting it forth as an example to all, yet especially places before the eyes of the religious: They had one heart and one soul (Acts iv). And that in the book of Psalms: God, who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house (Ps. lxvii). The monk must therefore beware in every way lest he either bear in his heart, or bring forth in deed, or show when overcome by anger, any grudge or hatred: because of what the Apostle says: For the anger of man does not work the justice of God (James ii); and that saying of the most wise Solomon: Anger rests in the bosom of the fool (Eccl. vii); and also that of the Apostle: Let all bitterness, and anger, and indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice (Eph. iv).
Chap. IV. That no woman is to enter the monastery.

For we believe it fitting to establish this: that no woman at all is to approach the monastery, even if she seems to seek it out of affection. Likewise we also cut off permission to approach from religious women or girls, lest perhaps any excuse be left to the less understanding: because a dwelling cannot long be secure with the enemy near or the foe neighbouring; especially since it comes into doubt by whom the public enemy is overcome, and in a secret fight, where there is nothing else left but either to conquer or to perish. But if some evident cause compels any of the brothers to hold a conversation, and that only with honourable women, far from the monastery, with the abbot knowing or permitting it, and witnesses being present, that is, two of the brothers joined with him, let them receive permission to converse: yet in such a way that the abbot is not ignorant of the matter about which the conversation took place.
Chap. V. On him who wishes to be a monk, how he is to be received.

If anyone comes seeking the religious life, intending to enter the monastery, let him not be joined to the fellowship of the monks unless a full year has first elapsed; or at least, if it seems good to the abbot to moderate this somewhat, not before the number of days of six months is completed: so that in so long a space he may show to those who do not know him what sort of man he will be; and by long observation it may become clear whether he has brought with him any harshness. But when he first comes to the monastery and asks to be received into the number of the monks, let him be asked whether he is free; and when he has satisfied the abbot with his first answer, let the following answer add whether he has decided to seek the monastery compelled by no cause other than devotion. After this, let the rule of the monastery be read to him at the abbot's order: so that afterwards he may meet nothing new or unaccustomed, whether he passes on intending to depart, or learns it intending to stay. Then let him receive a little cell near the monastery while he observes the appointed period, and let him expect his daily food from the monastery if he works among the rest: giving attention above all to reading and prayer, so that that almighty searcher of the soul and knower of secrets may deign to number him, by his merits, with his family of the holy congregation, and there may be, as it is written, one flock and one Shepherd (John x).
Chap. VI. That no monk or cleric is to be received to be kept.

We do not wish, we forbid, we prohibit that a monk or cleric of another place or monastery be received on any pretext whatever: foreseeing such things out of zeal for charity, lest, arising, they perhaps bring in some new scandal. For Scripture says: What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another (Tob. iv). For from this very often incurable disputes arise not only between abbots but also between monasteries, while one strives to defend the one he took in, and the other to recall the one he lost: and in the end, unless the one sought is returned to the one seeking him, and restitution for the one received appeases, as far as it can, the injury suffered, it comes about that, not according to the blessed Apostle (Rom. xii), they overcome evil with good, but rather both are overcome by one evil. Yet we have judged that this too should not be passed over: that if perhaps a monk or cleric of another place, as I said above, brings letters of his abbot or bishop in which it is clearly proven that he is not someone to be guarded against on account of vices, but sent for the love of God, he may then obtain to become a member of the congregation. If, however, it can in any way be believed that anyone wishes to be stripped of his own good, and another to be clothed with his nakedness.
Chap. VII. On the murmuring or detraction of monks.

That no one's murmuring or detraction, which is most habitual with monks, be heard in the congregation against the abbot or any other of the brothers: lest the wrath of God, which has often condemned a wretched people for this fault, be stirred up likewise to the destruction of a crowd of murmurers; and lest their own murmuring lose them the land of promise, which we rightly take as the place of future blessedness, which is owed by divine pledge. For here the psalm announces that the followers of this vice are to be condemned: The one who secretly slandered his neighbour, him I pursued (Ps. c). And again the Apostle, reproving, says: Whisperers, detractors, hateful to God (Rom. i). And again: These are querulous murmurers, walking according to their own desires, and their mouth speaks pride (Jude i).
Chap. VIII. On avoiding pride or elation.

That elation and pride be wholly avoided by monks, lest, by boasting, one's own loftiness fall, [rather than] be laid aside for God's sake. Abasement and humility are a great height. Otherwise, what will it be to have left the world, if he has not cut off its vanity from himself? What, to have chosen the solitary life, if he swells inwardly in heart? What progress in humility is there in the head, if he does not quickly cast these evils from himself, he who wishes to find a place to fall, rather than heeding that terrible saying of divine Scripture: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (I Pet. v). And that: With the proud eye and the insatiable heart I did not eat (Ps. c). And let him not be a forgetful hearer of that saying of the Apostle: Know this, that in the last days perilous times will come; and men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, elated, proud, blasphemers (II Tim. iii), and the rest that follows.
Chap. IX. On envy.

Envy, which is the greatest vice, let the monk above all shut out from the doors of his mind, and not allow the virginity of his soul to be corrupted by hidden spite: lest an adulterous admixture kill the good seed sown in his mind. But let him always stand like a strong man in the battle line, fighting back the weapons of envy with the shield of charity; and let him overcome the envious man chiefly in this, that he is not overcome by envy: not ignorant of the Scripture which says: By the envy of the devil death entered into the world (Wis. ii). And those who are of his party imitate him.
Chap. X. That a monk should not claim anything as his own.

We have also judged that this ought to be laid down: that none of the monks should dare to claim anything as his own apart from the fellowship of the brothers; so that even in those things which are his, he should believe that he has no more right than the others. For when he has subjected himself to another's power, he has transferred everything along with himself into another's power. Whatever property, then, he has brought with him, having sought the fellowship of the monks, and as soon as he has been joined to the body of the congregation as a member, let him at once recognise that everything has passed into common ownership, and let him judge that only to be his own which he possesses undivided with the brothers. For the reading of the Acts of the Apostles also recalls that the faithful of Christ lived in this way at the time of the rising Church: No one, it says, said that anything of his goods was his own; but they had all things in common (Acts iv).
Chap. XI. That no monk should be ignorant of letters.

Anyone who wishes to claim the name of monk, let it not be permitted to him to be ignorant of letters. Moreover, let him hold all the psalms by heart, and let him not defend himself by any excuse whatever from being taken up with this holy study. Likewise those who, as is the custom, are sent from the congregation as herdsmen of the flocks shall also take care to give time to the psalms as the others do: lest they be found lesser in that which is greater, and to their confusion that example be applied to them: But the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God (I Cor. ii).
Chap. XII. That the psalms be sung in order on all days.

That at all times the psalms be chanted in order through to the end of the Psalter: privately, however, for one's own reward, apart from the public course of the Lord's psalmody, as much as [he can] on each day, so that he may yet offer praises to God knowingly by hidden rumination. Likewise it will also be fitting to keep vigil by night with frequent psalms, with prayer added, so that this may be fulfilled: By day I have cried out, and by night before you (Ps. lxxxvii); and this: On his law he will meditate day and night (Ps. i).
Chap. XIII. On vigils.

Whenever a night vigil for entreating God is either requested out of devotion or owed on account of a feast, let none of the monks, except for certain sickness or necessity, presume to be absent if he is at hand. Lest, growing used to labouring more heavily under inner weariness, the spiritual soul die while the flesh lives: but rather, eager for that promise, let him strive both to seek and to find him who said: I love those who love me, and those who keep watch for me in the morning will find me (Prov. viii). And in the psalm also it is contained: Then they sought him, and turned, and came to him before daybreak (Ps. lxxvii). For we urge that all without exception rise daily for matins, if this is not thought superfluous; but for the night office on all days let all rise so quickly and together that, as all run together at once, no one is found to have come later. But whoever is caught acting against this statute shall fast alone for as many days as the hours he was unwilling to keep vigil with the brothers.
Chap. XIV. On the clothing of monks.

Let the monk not seek clothing beyond what suffices: let him receive no more than the abbot sees to be necessary for daily use; for the Lord says to the disciples: Do not have two tunics (Luke vii [sic]): which two tunics we ought to understand are to be counted not by number, if they seem necessary on account of winter, but if they have been kept beyond use. Whatever, then, is surplus will be reckoned as belonging to another: for whatever a greedy possessor locks away, the chest makes more use of it than the owner. That this be avoided, the blessed Apostle rises up as our greatest witness, who says: Having food and clothing, with these we are content. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, and many desires, both useless and harmful, which plunge men into ruin and perdition. The root of all evils is greed: craving which, they have made shipwreck of the faith and have pierced themselves with many sorrows. But you, O man of God, flee these things: pursue justice, piety, faith, charity, patience, gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith: lay hold of eternal life, to which you were called, and have confessed the good confession before many witnesses. I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who bore witness under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the commandment without stain, irreproachable, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (I Tim. vi). Strive therefore, brothers, that what is written to one man, that is, to Timothy, be kept by one congregation.
Chap. XV. That no one be baptised in the monastery.

We have considered that it is not necessary for little children to be baptised in the monastery, as is observed in the other monasteries; nor for a monk in any place to receive anyone's children from the holy font: lest, as tends to happen, he be gradually joined to their parents by an unlawful or shameful familiarity. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be corrected as a transgressor of the rule.
Chap. XVI. That no one apart from the abbot have a separate cell.

Let it be permitted to none of the monks, apart from the abbot, to have a cell of his own, either for living in or for any other use whatever. Craftsmen, however, may have [one] for working only, and these only those to whom it is granted by the abbot's appointment: for let one dwelling and one house enclose the whole congregation. But those whom bodily frailty weakens, whom sickness has beset, their infirmity being known, while they recover their former vigour in soundness of body, let them meanwhile be separated from the congregation in a dwelling assigned within the monastery, and only a suitable one: so that the very removal from the congregation may bring health more quickly.
Chap. XVII. That the monks have a prior or a formarius under the abbot's authority.

We have decreed that under the abbot there be appointed, for the abbot's relief, an energetic person who greatly loves discipline, to take up the worthy charge and name of prior: so that the honour may be less burdensome to him, while, the labour being divided, the daily care is borne by two. And therefore it will be right that, at the abbot's command, reverence and obedience be shown to him. And after the prior we spoke of above, who should be a pattern in good things, we have resolved to form a regular formarius [i.e. instructor], so that, with this help added, the abbot, whose name is Father, may more easily reap rich fruits from the perfection of his sweet sons; yet let both know that they are under the authority of the abbot, with the rest and among the rest.
Chap. XVIII. On the passions of the martyrs which can be found, that they be read at their proper time without sloth hindering.

The acts of the martyrs, that is, the passions of the holy faithful, some of which have been compiled with care and set out in writing, we absolutely decree are to be read through in the oratory with all listening, at the time when the year's turning, by the laws of its course, brings back to us the day of their departure: so that the day may not pass idly and be held like the rest; that, just as the martyr's steadfastness then made it illustrious, so now the memory of the passion may commend it.
Chap. XIX. That reading be frequent in the monk's hands.

To rouse the sluggish minds of some, in whom divine reading often breeds distaste, so that they would rather choose to be occupied with idleness than drink salvation from the holy Scriptures so as to burn with spiritual fervour, it has been resolved that this certainly be added: that each monk, whether he does some work inside the monastery or outside, should not allow himself to pass even a single day fasting from divine reading. And when the hand rests from work, let the soul be cultivated by reading, all hearing the admonitions of blessed Paul to his disciple Timothy, who says: Attend to reading, exhortation, teaching (I Tim. iv). And again: All Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, for instructing in justice: that the man of God may be perfect, ready for every good work (II Thes. iii [sic]).
Chap. XX. On wandering or fugitive monks.

As it is not fitting for a monk to wander from place to place, so it is not proper; lest, caught in some vice, he slip away through delight in the world, so as to return to his vomit: while, by a relapse of the will, the old despiser of the world, rising up as a new lover of it, is twisted from the way of salvation and goes astray. Therefore we have determined this is to be observed: that, apart from those who are ordered by the abbot to make journeys here and there for the benefit of the monastery, no one presume to leave the monastery to stay in another place without the abbot's will, for any matter or necessity whatever, lest there apply to him what the Apostle says, writing of the younger widows: And at the same time, being idle, they learn to go about from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and busybodies, speaking what they ought not (I Tim. v). And therefore whoever, setting aside this ruling, departs in some act of defiance, so that he is found to have been its transgressor, the space of time he was absent from the monastery being reckoned, shall fast for double the number of days and be punished with condemnation, keeping to such a measure of food as the abbot imposes, with wine denied him daily. But a fugitive monk, who deserts discipline and destroys himself, it has been resolved to call back as a despiser.
Chap. XXI. That a brother should not lay hands on a brother.

That no monk, inflamed with anger, presume to lay hands on a monk, which is most shameful, apart from those to whom it belongs either to know the measure of correction or to hold judgement; lest, when one sins, the boldness of the rest to presume should grow, and so, the order of discipline being thrown into confusion and the law of living broken through, we lose one by one the rights of holy religion itself. Therefore whoever is found so unrestrained with his hands that he does not know how to hold back from what is forbidden, let those hands which he raised against his neighbour be wearied for a long time not only by fasting but also by constant work, so that from then on they may be lifted to God in prayer, not stretched out in fury against a brother. We decree, however, that pardon is to be given to him who asks, as the abbot may wish to moderate it, if, penance having gone before, he has also bathed his face with a flood of tears while he begs [pardon] for his guilt.
Chap. XXII. That monks should abstain from abuse and cursing.

That no abuse or cursing proceed from a monk's mouth, nor his tongue, loosed by the stirring of impatience, supply anything unbridled to the doors of the lips; but, when moved by anger, as is human, let him say: Set, Lord, a guard on my mouth, and a door enclosing my lips (Psal. cxl). Let him add this also: I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not offend with my tongue (Psal. xxxviii), having before his eyes that saying of the Apostle: For neither will the abusive possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. vi). If anyone, then, untamed in mind, breaks out in these things, let him be kept apart from conversation with all the brothers for thirty days, until, recognising that he has incurred solitude even in the midst of the congregation, he chooses to ask for pardon.
Chap. XXIII. That a monk should both cease and desist from swearing.

That the habit of swearing be removed entirely, if it can be done, from the conversation of monks; so that, even if according to human frailty they may perhaps be less able to guard against the sin of lying, they may at least avoid damnable perjury. These I ask and at the same time admonish to take care to make use of holy words, so that oaths may never be necessary. For how all ought to avoid the outrage of this vice we have learned from the admonition of the blessed apostle; for he says: Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth, or any other oath whatever. But let your word be yes, yes, no, no, so that you do not fall under judgement (Luc. v). And likewise that saying of divine Scripture: A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house (Eccli. xxiii). To these great and most evident proofs the reading of the Gospel also, which is the greatest fullness, likewise bears witness, the Lord saying to the disciples: You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not swear falsely; but you shall render your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be yes, yes, no, no; and whatever is more than these is from evil (Matth. v). Let it suffice, then, that we have taught by examples what is to be avoided, in place of inserting admonitions of our own.
Chap. XXIV. That a monk should laugh seldom.

I believe this also is fitting for monks: that they abstain from laughter, if not constantly, yet often. Hence if any of the brothers, in reading, looks for an example, let this alone suffice him: that we read that our Lord Jesus Christ wept, as the Gospel witnesses (Joan. xii), [but] we do not know that he laughed; he was saddened to tears, not loosened in laughter. Yet, lest anyone say that we have no testimony of reading apart from this, let him hear Solomon saying: Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes hold of the end of joy (Prov. xiv). And again: Anger is better than laughter, for by sadness of countenance the mind of the offender is corrected. The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is mirth (Eccl. vii). And again: The fool raises his voice in laughter, but the wise man will scarcely smile quietly (Eccli. xxi). Whoever, then, placed in the congregation, being, as usually happens, young in mind or in age, does not flee laughter and jokes, what else does he do but change from a monk into a publican? — [such men] as in the more populous cities assign themselves this task alone: to give their time to jokes, applause and guffaws. But I especially admonish all, and I command and establish this to be kept: that whenever a reading suited to souls devoted to God is recited publicly in the church or in the refectory or in any place, no one either be moved to laughter or move [others to it]. Likewise let them know that at that time idle tales are to be shunned. But if anyone, having been warned by the present notice, does not keep this, let the penalty of a three-day fast chastise him. This three days we wish no one to fulfil in a single fast, lest the discipline lack discretion in any respect; but we order the three fasts until evening to be separated by a daily meal. This we decree is also to be observed concerning the other fasts by which those at fault against the rule are corrected; provided, however, that the abbot does not see pride and obstinacy in the guilty monk, whoever he may be.
Chap. XXV. That a monk should entirely shun foul speech.

Let it be shameful for a monk, for love of chastity, to utter foul speech, avoiding words of lust, which, as they arouse the mind, so inflame the body. For the blessed Apostle says: Put away malice, blasphemy, foul speech from your mouth (Colos. iii). I ask, brothers, what less does he do than an adulterer, whose tongue shares in the sin? What less of lust has he practised who has defiled a chaste mouth with corruption of speech? And so that fear of condemnation may lay on all the duty of guarding against this filth, we decree that one guilty of this fault shall not have the Lord's communion, or the kiss of the brothers, for six months of the year.
Chap. XXVI. That monks should read daily until the third hour.

That at all times, until the third hour of the day, the monk, the senior as much as the lowliest, take care to give himself to reading, and only then, in the rest of the day, let the care of assigned work follow; except only the sick, on whom common infirmity does not allow this to be imposed beyond their own will, or rather strength. For those also whom the abbot has ordered, at the time of gathering in the crops, to do some work or labour in the morning hours will not be bound by this law; nor will they be thought to have acted against this ruling, when they have fulfilled what was commanded them for the sake of usefulness. For it is the custom of farmers to cut the dry grain when morning has scarcely returned, while it is still moist only from the falling dew, so that they may more easily snatch the less abundant crop from the heats that follow, while at the start of the day they keep the mildness of the soft air. For I know it is often done deliberately that, while the light is still uncertain, before, as we might say, the heat of the sun's orb has drunk dry the crop gathered into sheaves, its harvest escapes with the fruits the flames of the fiery radiance. If this, then, has been observed also by monks who are engaged in work, as we said above, they are not to be declared transgressors of the rule, for the sake of the advantage of the work.
Chap. XXVII. That no monk should eat or drink before the third hour.

That none of the monks, except the sick, before the third hour of the day is completed, presume to eat or drink, whether asking or asked, even if the occasion sought out for gluttony is propped up by the arrival of some neighbour or friend — that is, at the time when the customary fasts are released by relaxation. After this hour, however, let him extend the decision to eat until the sixth, if either his friend or his stomach allows. But at this meal let him seek and make one or two brothers his companions, so that, while he is seen to be open through this sharing and courtesy, he does not appear to have slipped in by stealth.
Chap. XXVIII. That a monk should do some work daily.

We decree that a monk who passes a day without working, apart from fixed solemnities or evident sickness, is to be excluded from the common table, as the blessed Apostle commands: He who does not work, let him not eat. Yet we foresee the excuses of the useless that will follow, and therefore we set a limit for the idle. For one of such men is going to say: I cannot work, because, having lost the strength of youth, I am an old man, feeble for everything; another: Nor can I, because I am already broken by infirmity; a third too is going to say, if he can be found: I cannot either, because constant labours have worn me down, the length of journeys has shaken me, the charge entrusted to me has taken away my strength, the business laid on me has stripped me of my vigour. But let the word of reason meet them as an opponent, refuting them and saying: If anyone is not able to apply himself to work, let him give himself more readily to reading; whoever does not cultivate a field, let him worship God doubly; and among other things let him seek this art too, that he who does not mark out the earth with the plough may paint the page with his finger. Let no one, then, think that he brings forward a cause of just excuse for doing less work, because he who, as we said above, is not able to practise agriculture can read, write, which is the foremost work, also see to the catching of fish, weave nets, make shoes for the brothers, or do and carry out other things which are similar. Whoever, then, does not choose from all these some work by which to be occupied, let him be content to endure hunger with reproach.
Chap. XXIX. That a monk should speak sparingly.

That a monk should keep restraint in speaking in every conversation, because of what Scripture says: In much speaking you will not escape sin (Prov. 10). And again in the Gospel: Do not speak much, like the heathen (Matt. 6). It is also found in the psalm: A talkative man will not be set straight upon the earth (Ps. 139). And so, whoever you are, brother, let your words be few. And not only this, but let the presence of the abbot or of any other elder impose silence on you as well, so that you do not presume to break silence unless questioned or ordered by him, obeying the Scripture which says: Before you hear, do not answer; and do not thrust yourself into the midst of the elders (Ecclus. 11). We declare most plainly that this is to be observed at meals as well.
Chap. XXX. That the abbot does no work except of his own will.

That if the abbot does not work as the others do, let no one dare to find fault with him, because it is more fitting for him to give his time to reading, by which he may teach the others daily, by which he may make those entrusted to him learned, by which he may order all with constant holy admonition. Yet he ought to take care that whenever a book is not in his hands he makes himself a sharer, according to his strength, in any of the brothers' work, so that, even if no one dares to call him idle, no one may murmur in silence that he is disdainful.
Chap. XXXI. That monks are not permitted to use a linen tunic.

That a monk, however delicate his body, should not use linen next to the bare body, because it is unfitting that he should cherish with soft clothing the flesh, which always grows proud by the flaw of its nature, and flatter it as if it were weaker, when daily it is stirred up like some new and very strong warrior to storm the soul. For it renews its strength to make war against the soul as often as, like a rebellious slave, it has received some relaxation. Of this struggle the blessed Apostle says: The flesh lusts against the spirit (Gal. 5). And again: I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members (Rom. 7). And again: There was given to me a goad of my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me, for which I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness (II Cor. 12). And again: If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live (Rom. 8). Whoever, then, loves that life, let him crush the flesh that is to die; and let him, like a tireless and constant conqueror, so bind it in daily wrestling with certain hard bonds of discipline that it does [not] fight against the soul on account of even a slight relaxation, following the teaching and example of the Apostle, who says: I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself become reprobate (I Cor. 9).
Chap. XXXII. That monks' clothes should not have choice scents.

Let a monk take care not to have fragrance in his clothes, or excessive brightness for the sake of pride, but rather follow the Apostle who says: We are the good odour of Jesus Christ (II Cor. 2). Let him also avoid in them, and not seek to have, a white colour or one too red, through which the beauty of the body is often commended to onlookers, to their ruin; lest he carry with him the evidence of his own vanity, and, God forbid, while he labours to adorn his body for a time with clothes soon to wear out, he care nothing for the ornaments of the soul, which could be eternal. For the divine Scripture rebukes those who do such things thus: Do not glory in the wearing of clothes, and do not be lifted up in the day of glory (Ecclus. 11). As for shoes, we decree that you keep the custom of the other monks. But this too must be seen to: that the foot be bound with its laces in moderation, so that it does not have many [knots] tied tight as a sign of vanity, but, more holily, sits loose in a looser binding; so that in all things simplicity, with holiness as its companion, may commend to God the man whom it sees possessed by love of him, a proven despiser of the world.
Chap. XXXIII. That monks should have beds singly.

That two, however close neighbours or friends, should not be held in one bed, for the sake of secret prayer, which is better directed to the Lord with no witness; so that the contrite mind may believe that greater freedom of praying is granted to it, while it fears no one either as witness or as judge of its vigil. By watching, then, praying and singing psalms, let each one take care to yield the smallest portion of the night to sleep, so that he who is free of a companion may not be deceived by [sleep]: for he cannot rightly claim a bed of his own at all unless he keeps watch. It seems we must also fulfil what the prophet sings to us by way of admonition: Every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with tears (Ps. 6). And again: In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places, and bless the Lord (Ps. 133). And this: I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and kept your law (Ps. 118). So that each devout man may fulfil this more profitably in the leisure granted, he will, as we said above, be the sole possessor of his bed, having with him, by a better exchange, instead of a brother as bedfellow, the Lord who keeps watch.
Chap. XXXIV. That a monk should not hunt.

Among the other pleasures of the world let the monk know that he is forbidden to practise hunting, and that he must not engage in dangerous combat with wild beasts without profit, since he ought rather to know that vices are to be slain instead of beasts. And so let neither the custom of the place, nor the nearness and convenience of the woods, nor the easy and accessible ascent of a mountain, the hollows of the valleys, the hidden places of the groves, the thickets of the land, entice him to undertake the task of so fruitless a labour. For he ought, mindful of the Apostle's saying, not to bring harm upon religion, since he admonishes that each one should remain before God in the calling in which he was called (Eph. 4). Let him judge, then, that the good course of his life perishes in vain coursings, and let him beware of doing himself harm; lest, setting aside the monk, he himself be caught in the catching of wild beasts, and, entangled in worldly desires, the hunter of wild beasts himself become the adversary's quarry. But let him rejoice to give his time to God alone, whom he seeks; to serve continually him whom he has chosen, knowing that we are admonished thus by the precept of the Gospel: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (Matt. 4). And elsewhere: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps. 26). Let him strive, then, setting all else aside, how he may please him continually with all service, so that he may make him a sharer in his kingdom whom he sees to be wholly his worshipper. Yet we have thought that this too should not be omitted: if perhaps the more violent wild beasts lie in wait among the fruits for one seeking his food by his own labour, let the fierceness of dogs fittingly frighten them off, solely to make good the damage to the fruits; let him delight rather in driving them away than in pursuing them, so that he may appear to be a lover not of hunting but rather of the fruits.
Chap. XXXV. That a monk should not presume even to touch fruit without permission.

Whatever monk, without permission, plucks a fruit of any kind still hanging on its tree, merely for greed's sake, or one fallen to the ground, or [dares], as often happens, to violate the first-fruits of other produce in the play of an unrestrained gullet, being like old Adam, the first man, let him do fitting penance by a fast, his greed being punished in like manner; as if, in place of paradise, he were judged unworthy of the meal. And unless he first obtains pardon by the forgiveness of all the brothers, let him not be permitted to come to table; for it is just that he who took from all what was common should ask the indulgence of all. All, then, must take care that whatever is assigned for human food, if it falls to any of the brothers to receive or even to find it, he keep it untouched in all good faith before he either brings it to table or hands it over to the storeroom; avoiding stealing for himself by tasting the food common to all; and lest, though no companion is with him, his gullet should be his companion for losing his innocence or for taking plunder. Therefore the congregation will always have a single property, so that all things belong to all, and everything to everyone.
Chap. XXXVI. That the abbot should not presume to free a slave of the monastery.

The abbot will not have licence to make a slave of the monastery free without the consent of all the monks, unless he hands over to all the brothers at once, from his own means, a substitute of like worth and age; for the slave of many cannot pass to freedom by the release of one, nor become a freedman unless all with one mind release him, since it is plain that he has as many masters as there are monks. Chap. XXXVII. On how the abbot ought to conduct himself.

That the abbot should be commended to all the monks over whom he presides by vigour indeed, but [also] by gentleness, and rather by his life, so that they fear him more as holy than as severe; and fear in him more that he is first in merit than that he is foremost in rank. Let him keep measure in correction, and restraint in familiarity; and he will be so balanced in all his ways that he calls with gentleness and chastises with fear, making himself the more loved by all because he hates vices. For his whole manner of life will be like a laid foundation, so that whoever wishes to draw near to God in merit by imitating him may be built up upon him. No one will be condemned by him by [mere] power, but by reason; yet no one will be so familiar with him as to presume more than others, nor so out of favour as not to return to pardon once his contrition is complete. For it befits him who is feared by all to fear for all, and to take care with all zeal and diligence that no one of those whom he has taken under his own care to govern should leave their number through any mishap. Therefore he must come to the aid of the monks' sicknesses with many medicines, and apply the remedy of spiritual care to the illnesses of minds: that is, if he sees someone proud, let him offer the draught of humility by constant exhortation; if [he sees someone] wrathful, let him offer him the ointment of patience; if [he sees someone] pursuing falsehood, let him administer the antidote of truth, stirred in this by the admonitions of the blessed Apostle, who says: Attend [to yourself and to teaching], persist in them: for in doing this you will save both [yourself] and those who hear you (II Tim. iv). And again to Timothy: Hold the pattern of sound words which you heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus (II Tim. i). And again: But you, be watchful, labour in all things, do the work of an evangelist; fulfil your ministry (II Tim. iv). Likewise blessed Peter writes: I beseech the elders who are among you, I a fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and partaker of the glory that is to be revealed, feed the flock of God which is among you (I Pet. v). And he added: Not as lording it over the clergy, but be a pattern to the flock, so that when the chief of shepherds appears, you may receive the flowering and unfading crown of glory. The most holy Jeremiah also says in the person of the Lord: [I will give] you shepherds after my own heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and teaching (Jer. iii). And again: Thus says Adonai the Lord to the shepherds of Israel: Do the shepherds feed themselves? And he adds: Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord; thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I myself [am] against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hands (Ezek. xxxiv). And the same Lord in the Gospel, asking Peter, the chief of the apostles, whether he loved him, adds: Feed my sheep (John xxi). It is plain, then, brother, whoever you are who are seen to preside over monks, that a great burden has been laid on you with the honour; so that, while you are first in dignity, you toil laden with the weight of all. Therefore run the path of the right road that leads to heaven; show the flock an unobstructed track, and go before it also in the steps of holiness; and strive so that whoever follows you as leader in the steps of imitation does not go astray; so that you may be seen to have fulfilled the admonitions of the apostolic saying, which runs: Be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity (I Tim. iv). And again: Take care to show yourself to God an approved workman who need not be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth (II Tim. ii). So we set down this chapter for you, abbot, as if more particularly, so that you may not grieve at being passed over in the words of the Rule, and may thus recognise yourself as one of the congregation: warning, and indeed beseeching you before God, that, keeping all these things with fervent zeal, you also observe, for the sake of example, the other things that have been said to the rest.
Chap. XXXVIII. At what times the abbot should attend to the kitchen, and likewise to the washing of feet.

Three times a year, that is, on the day of the Lord's Nativity, likewise on the first [day] of Easter, and also on the feast of our own patron, the holy and most blessed martyr Ferreolus, ever to be venerated, or at any rate [on the feast of those] saints in whose names that place has been consecrated, the abbot shall enter the kitchen to prepare food for the congregation; and there, taking up the service of a junior, let him serve the tables and show a pattern of humility in [bringing] the dishes; bending himself willingly to this holy abasement, which makes him greater than the others while it makes him their equal. For his authority gains so much the more among all, the further he descends to lower things by sharing equally in service. He shall also be eager to wash the feet of the brothers, and of pilgrims too, often, imitating the divine example; fulfilling the Lord's command, and giving the monks an example by deeds rather than by words. For the Lord too says to the disciples in the Gospel: If I, the Lord and master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also should do (John xiii). Let all the monks, then, with following hearts imitate the abbot when he does these things, and in the common observance of this chapter: so much so that, at appointed times and in separate turns, they serve one another, being careful about the preparation of food, and are masters of each other in equality of service.
Chap. XXXIX. The chastisement of monks for many excesses.

This chapter has undertaken to chastise the negligences of monks with many admonitions. Nor does it seek to condemn persons so much as faults. Let them be made clean, then, and as it were purged of the defilement of all vices, by the love of soundness, the striving for perfection, the expectation of truth, the promise of glory, the everlastingness of life, and that dwelling with the Creator in which we believe; of which the Apostle speaks thus: We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, and so we shall be always with the Lord (I Thess. iv).

The word of correction, then, for those who sow quarrels among the brothers is this: that if faith does not draw them from so perverse a way, they are to be struck not only by the sentence of the abbot but also by the dislike of all, until they abandon their habitual error. Of these the evangelist Luke records that the Lord said: It is impossible that scandals should not come; but woe to him through whom they come: it is better for him if a millstone be put about his neck and he be cast into the sea (Luke xvii).

But to those who, after correction, attacking the judgements of the elders, strive to excuse their sin, and, at the memory of their fault, pass not to penance but to an excessive hardness of indignation, this sentence applies: that until they are recalled from their set purpose and lay aside the swelling of their mind by manifest amendment, they are to be subjected altogether to hard discipline at the abbot's discretion; for they did not say: I acknowledge my sin (Psalm l); but they said what is read of the rebellious in Isaiah the prophet: There is no one who does penance for his sin, saying, What have I done? (Jer. viii)

Those who put themselves before their seniors, and are not ashamed to seize the places of others through the vice of pride, and contradict the Lord's precepts, by which we are commanded thus: Whoever wishes to become greater among you, let him be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you, shall be your slave (Matt. xx), are to be shamed by the rebuke of the abbot and also of the rest, and recalled to their own place which they had left; and we decree that they be promoted to a higher rank only rather late, lest, with dignity added, the presumption rooted in them grow strong.

This also we establish: that when the brothers are gathered at table, no one should presume [upon] or seize another's portion of what is served, nor importunately plunge his hand into the dish more often than the others, because of that [saying] of the Apostle: One is hungry, and another is drunk (I Cor. xi). And again: Food for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them (I Cor. vi). And again: The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but justice and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. xiv). And again: For such do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly (Rom. xvi). And again: Whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. iii). We also read in the psalm, [a thing which be] far from monks too: Their food was still in their mouth, and the wrath of God rose up against them (Psalm lxxvii). Whoever, then, transgresses this statute, it will rest with the abbot's judgement by how many fasts his violence at table is to be judged.

As for drunkenness, I think it superfluous to warn a monk, since, even if he takes a little wine, he turns aside from his set purpose of mortifying the body. Yet because monks cannot fail to know what the Apostle writes to Timothy, saying: Use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses (II Tim. iii): let them accept as much wine as is offered them each day, according to the means of the monastery, by the abbot's order or allowance, and ask for nothing more at all. This we also establish is to be observed regarding the other rations. For we show by the testimonies of Scripture that drunkenness is forbidden even to those who live in the world, since the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: Do not, he says, be drunk with wine, in which is wantonness (Eph. v). And also the Prophet: Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong at mixing strong drink (Isa. v). And again: Woe to those who rise early in the morning and pursue strong drink, who wait for evening to be heated with wine. And therefore, if a monk should ever happen to be seen drunk, which it is a sin even to say, I, zealous for him and full of anger, command that he be suspended from drinking wine for thirty days: so that his soul, clogged by the infusion, may be emptied by digestion in this space [of time].

Therefore those monks whom the end of even a single day finds at odds, who drag out their quarrels until evening and do not shut out hatred before the sun knows its setting, who through disobedience contradict the Apostle when he says: Let not the sun go down upon your anger (Eph. iv), we decree are to be worn down by abstinence for as long as it takes them to turn to true concord by voluntary satisfaction. After a long scandal they are not to be allowed to make peace in secret, lest the purity of charity admit anything feigned; but let the reconciliation of those whose discord was open be public. So, with all the brothers standing by, let them ask pardon of each other: for each is marked as guilty by the long enmity, since either the one ceased to ask forgiveness, or the other, wishing to be entreated, did not forgive. And so the one has remained impious, the other impenitent: this one to be condemned for his anger, that one for his fault. Therefore let the one who was offended not keep his anger in contempt of the Gospel, but quickly have recourse to that example: Forgive, and you will be forgiven (Luke vi). And to that [saying] of the Apostle: Put on, as the elect of God and beloved, a heart of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another: as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also [forgive] (Col. iii). But let the one who inflicted the injury be swiftly frightened by this example: The Lord executes judgement for those who suffer injury (Ps. cxlv). And elsewhere: What a man sows, that he will also reap (Gal. vi).

One guilty of theft, if we can still call him a monk, we order to be subjected to the lash like an adulterer, and to be sentenced to severe affliction, giving him the same sentence as the fornicator, since he too indulged his lust when he stole. For not unfittingly do we call those alike whom we find placed side by side in the sacred reading. Thus the Lord says through the Prophet: There is no knowledge of God upon the earth (Hos. iv). And a little after: Theft and adultery have overflowed. And again in the psalm: If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you cast your lot with adulterers (Ps. xliii). We read also in the Gospel that the Lord said: Fornications, thefts; and without delay he added: These are the things that defile a man (Matt. xv). From these the slaves of these crimes can surely understand that, just as these vices rule them equally, so equal punishment is also due.

And so that, most beloved brothers in Christ, you may not grow negligent through forgetfulness of anything written above, read it over once every thirty days with all gathered together, that is, on the calends.
